nodes.label: Early Islamic Iraq
nodes.full: What precedes: Baghdad the world city, the Sawad the granary, the geonim and catholicos at the head of their faiths, and a caliph already a figurehead by 945. See iraq-632-945.
nodes.src: background — see the folio iraq-632-945.

nodes.label: Ilkhanid and Jalayirid Iraq
nodes.full: The aftermath: a wrecked frontier province of a Mongol state ruled from Tabriz, the canals gone, the caliphate finished — the shrine cities and the Sufi orders the institutions that carry on. See iraq-1258-1534.
nodes.src: background — see the folio iraq-1258-1534.

nodes.label: The Seljuk empire
nodes.full: The Turkish sultanate centred on Isfahan and Hamadan whose military governor rules Baghdad — the source of the regularised iqtaʿ, the state madrasa, the Sunni revival, and the Turkmen who settle the north.
nodes.src: background — A. C. S. Peacock, 'The Great Seljuk Empire' (2015).

nodes.label: The Fatimid and Crusader world
nodes.full: Shia Cairo and its Ismaili daʿwa, the castle of Alamut, the Frankish states on the Levant coast, and the counter-jihad mounted from Mosul and Aleppo — the rivals and the wars that Baghdad mostly watched.
nodes.src: background — Carole Hillenbrand, 'The Crusades: Islamic Perspectives' (1999).

nodes.label: The Mongol world
nodes.full: The Eurasian empire reaching from China to Russia — Hulagu's army, the pax Mongolica, the Nestorian and Buddhist elite of the early Ilkhans, and the force that ends the caliphate.
nodes.src: background — Rashid al-Din, 'Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh'.

nodes.label: The Buyid amirs in the caliph's name
nodes.full: The Buyids were Shia mountaineers from the Caspian who took Baghdad in 945 and ruled it for 110 years, keeping the Sunni Abbasid caliph on his throne as a source of legitimacy and a puppet. Adud al-Dawla, at the height in the 970s, revived the old Persian title King of Kings, rebuilt the flood-wrecked city, and endowed a great hospital. After him the dynasty fell apart in the quarrels of its own soldiers.
nodes.src: Miskawayh, 'Tajārib al-Umam'; John Donohue, 'The Buwayhid Dynasty in Iraq' (2003).

nodes.label: The Seljuk sultans take Baghdad
nodes.full: Tughril Beg, chief of the Oghuz Turks who had overrun Iran, entered Baghdad in 1055, ended the Buyids, and had the caliph name him sultan — 'king of east and west'. The Seljuks held real power for a century through a military governor, the shihna, stationed in the city; the caliph was left the Friday sermon and the robes of investiture. When the sultanate broke up, the office of caliph was still there to be reclaimed.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, 'al-Kāmil'; A. C. S. Peacock, 'The Great Seljuk Empire' (2015).

nodes.label: Nizam al-Mulk and the vizieral state
nodes.full: For thirty years the Persian vizier Nizam al-Mulk ran the Seljuk empire for two young sultans. He regularised the iqta, wrote a famous manual of statecraft, and founded a chain of state madrasas — the Nizamiyya — to train Sunni scholars and officials and to counter the Isma'ili underground. He and his master Malik-Shah both died in 1092, one by an assassin's knife, and the empire began to come apart.
nodes.src: Nizam al-Mulk, 'Siyāsatnāma'; the assassination in Ibn al-Athir; Peacock (2015).

nodes.label: The caliphs recover Iraq
nodes.full: As the Seljuk sultanate of Iraq dissolved into feuding princes, the caliph al-Muqtafi did what no Abbasid had done for two centuries: he raised his own army, drove the sultan's garrison out of Baghdad, and made central Iraq an actual caliphal state again. His successors held and extended it. The institution that had been a ceremonial fiction since 945 was, briefly, a government once more.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, 'al-Kāmil'; Angelika Hartmann, 'an-Nāṣir li-Dīn Allāh' (1975), on the recovery.

nodes.label: al-Nasir li-Din Allah — the last strong caliph
nodes.full: Al-Nasir reigned forty-five years and rebuilt a real territorial state in Iraq. Lacking an army to match the sultans, he ruled by prestige and network: he took over the urban chivalric brotherhoods, the futuwwa, made himself their head, and sent the belt of membership to rulers across the Muslim world as a bond of allegiance. He also opened the correspondence with the Mongols that his grandson would not know how to handle.
nodes.src: Angelika Hartmann, 'an-Nāṣir li-Dīn Allāh (1180–1225)' (1975).

nodes.label: al-Mustansir, al-Musta'sim and the end
nodes.full: Al-Mustansir built the Mustansiriyya, a madrasa teaching all four Sunni schools under one roof, and campaigned against the first Mongol probes. His son al-Musta'sim, a cultivated and weak man with a divided court, could neither fight Hulagu nor come to terms with him. In February 1258 the Mongols took the city, and had the caliph rolled in a carpet and trampled to death by horses.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Fuwati (attrib.), 'al-Ḥawādith al-Jāmiʿa'; Rashid al-Din, 'Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh'.

nodes.label: The shihna and the soldiery
nodes.full: Under the sultanate the real governor of Baghdad was the shihna, the military commander who held the citadel, kept order, collected what taxes he could, and answered to the sultan in Isfahan or Hamadan, not to the caliph across the city. The office and the Turkish troops behind it were the everyday face of foreign rule, and their pay demands and factional fights set the rhythm of the city's politics.
nodes.src: George Makdisi, 'Ibn ʿAqīl et la résurgence de l'islam traditionaliste' (1963); Ibn al-Jawzi, 'al-Muntaẓam'.

nodes.label: Hulagu and the Ilkhanate
nodes.full: Hulagu, brother of the Great Khan, was sent west with a huge army, destroyed the Assassins' castle of Alamut in 1256, and reached Baghdad the next winter. The city held out a fortnight, surrendered, and was given over to a week of massacre and plunder. Iraq became a frontier province of the Ilkhanate, a Mongol state ruled from Azerbaijan — governed, for the first time in its history, from outside the land entirely.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din, 'Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh'; John Andrew Boyle, 'The Death of the Last ʿAbbāsid Caliph' (1961).

nodes.label: The Sunni–Shia street wars of Buyid Baghdad
nodes.full: Under Shia amirs and a Sunni caliph, Baghdad's quarters fought each other. The Shia of Karkh and the Sunni neighbourhoods rioted every year around the mourning of Ashura and the feast of Ghadir, which the Buyids had made public; gangs of armed young men, the ayyarun, ran protection and arson; whole markets burned. The sectarian map of the modern city was drawn in these decades.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Jawzi, 'al-Muntaẓam'; Simha Sabari, 'Mouvements populaires à Bagdad' (1981).

nodes.label: The Basasiri revolt and the Fatimid year
nodes.full: A Turkish general, al-Basasiri, went over to the Fatimids of Cairo, seized Baghdad in 1058, and for the best part of a year had the Friday sermon preached in the name of the Shia caliph of Egypt while the Abbasid al-Qa'im was held prisoner up the Euphrates. Tughril Beg marched back, killed al-Basasiri, and restored the caliph in 1060. It was the nearest the Fatimids ever came to winning the whole game.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, 'al-Kāmil'; George Makdisi, 'The Marriage of Ṭughril Beg' (1970).

nodes.label: The succession wars and the atabegs
nodes.full: After Malik-Shah the Seljuk house fought itself for a century, its armies tramping back and forth across Iraq, its provinces breaking off under the guardians of its child-princes — the atabegs, of whom the line at Mosul, Zangi and his son Nur al-Din, grew strongest. The last Seljuk sultan of Iraq was killed in 1194, leaving the caliph and the atabeg states to divide what was left.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, 'al-Kāmil' and 'al-Bāhir'; A. C. S. Peacock, 'The Great Seljuk Empire' (2015).

nodes.label: The caliph killed in the field
nodes.full: The caliph al-Mustarshid tried to turn recovered Baghdad into real independence, marched an army against the Seljuk sultan, was beaten near Hamadan, and was murdered in the sultan's camp in 1135 — by Nizari assassins, it was said, with the sultan's connivance. His son was deposed and killed within three years. The bid for a fighting caliphate was checked in blood, and then, a generation later, quietly renewed.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, 'al-Kāmil'; Ibn al-Jawzi, 'al-Muntaẓam'.

nodes.label: The Nizari assassins in Iraq
nodes.full: From the castle of Alamut in the Iranian mountains the Nizari Isma'ilis waged a war of the dagger on the Sunni establishment — beginning with Nizam al-Mulk in 1092 and taking in viziers, judges, generals and two caliphs. The threat shaped policy: the madrasa was partly a weapon against them, and al-Nasir kept up a wary correspondence with Alamut until Hulagu wiped it out on his way to Baghdad.
nodes.src: Farhad Daftary, 'The Ismāʿīlīs: Their History and Doctrines' (2007); Ibn al-Athir, 'al-Kāmil'.

nodes.label: The Mongol sack of Baghdad
nodes.full: Hulagu's army invested Baghdad in late January 1258, broke the eastern wall with catapults within days, and accepted the caliph's surrender on 10 February. Then came a week of killing and burning — the death toll put by the sources anywhere from two hundred thousand upward — the libraries thrown in the Tigris, the mosques and shrines plundered, the caliph executed. Five hundred years of the Abbasid Caliphate ended in that week.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din, 'Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh'; the Syriac account of Bar Hebraeus; Nassima Neggaz, 'The Falls of Baghdad in 1258 and 2003' (2013).

nodes.label: al-Mawardi and the theory of the powerless caliph
nodes.full: Writing under Buyid rule, the jurist al-Mawardi set down a working theory of the caliphate: the caliph remained the sole legitimate source of authority, but he could delegate real power — even to a warlord who had simply seized it, an 'amir by usurpation' — and that delegation, and the diploma that recorded it, made the seizure lawful. It was the fiction that let the system function for two more centuries.
nodes.src: al-Mawardi, 'al-Aḥkām al-Sulṭāniyya'; Hamilton Gibb, 'Al-Mawardi's Theory of the Caliphate' (1937).

nodes.label: The sultanate and the manual of rule
nodes.full: The Seljuks split what the early caliphs had held together: the caliph kept religious legitimacy, the sultan took worldly power, and each needed the other. Nizam al-Mulk's Book of Government laid out how the worldly half should work — a standing army paid by land assignment, an intelligence service, a suspicious eye on the bureaucracy and the heretics. The division of caliph and sultan became permanent Sunni doctrine.
nodes.src: Nizam al-Mulk, 'Siyāsatnāma' (tr. Darke); Ann Lambton, 'State and Government in Medieval Islam' (1981).

nodes.label: The madrasa as an instrument of state
nodes.full: Nizam al-Mulk's Baghdad Nizamiyya, opened in 1067, was a state-endowed college with salaried chairs, stipends for students, and a purpose: to mass-produce Sunni scholars and officials of the Shafi'i school and the Ash'ari creed, and to fight Isma'ilism with argument. The Mustansiriyya of 1234 went further, teaching all four Sunni schools under one roof. The madrasa fixed the shape of Islamic learning.
nodes.src: George Makdisi, 'The Rise of Colleges: Institutions of Learning in Islam and the West' (1981).

nodes.label: The iqta becomes the whole system
nodes.full: Under the Seljuks the iqtaʿ stopped being an expedient and became the normal way an army existed: the tax revenue of a district was assigned to an officer, who collected it, kept his troops from it, and in practice passed it to his son. The muqtaʿ was the local lord, with little reason to invest in the land beyond the next harvest. Central control of the Sawad's revenue, and of its canals, effectively ended.
nodes.src: Claude Cahen, 'L'évolution de l'iqṭāʿ du IXe au XIIIe siècle' (1953); A. C. S. Peacock (2015).

nodes.label: The waqf that built the city
nodes.full: The medieval Islamic city was largely built and kept up not by the state but by the waqf — a perpetual endowment, a donor's property tied forever to the upkeep of a madrasa, a hospital, a Sufi lodge, a fountain, a bridge or a soup kitchen. Baghdad's institutions ran on it. It let private wealth create durable public goods in a polity whose rulers came and went with the soldiery.
nodes.src: George Makdisi, 'The Rise of Colleges' (1981); Yaacov Lev, 'Charity, Endowments, and Charitable Institutions in Medieval Islam' (2005).

nodes.label: al-Nasir's futuwwa order
nodes.full: Baghdad's neighbourhoods had long had brotherhoods of young men — the futuwwa — with initiation rites, a code of honour, and a talent for street violence. Al-Nasir, needing influence he could not enforce with an army, reorganised them into a single graded order under his own headship and sent the initiation trousers and cup to sultans and princes abroad, making membership a bond of loyalty to him. It was diplomacy dressed as chivalry.
nodes.src: Angelika Hartmann, 'an-Nāṣir li-Dīn Allāh' (1975); Claude Cahen, 'Mouvements populaires et autonomisme urbain' (1959).

nodes.label: The Baghdad school of Twelver theology
nodes.full: Buyid protection gave Twelver Shi'ism a century in the open in Baghdad. The mourning of Ashura and the feast of Ghadir became public rituals; Adud al-Dawla rebuilt the shrines of Najaf, Karbala and Kazimayn in stone; and a brilliant generation of scholars — al-Shaykh al-Mufid, al-Sharif al-Radi who assembled the sayings of Ali into the Nahj al-Balagha, and al-Tusi — turned the imams' teaching into a systematic theology and law.
nodes.src: Tamima Bayhom-Daou, 'Shaykh Mufid' (2005); Moojan Momen, 'An Introduction to Shiʿi Islam' (1985).

nodes.label: The Seljuk restoration of Sunnism
nodes.full: The Seljuks came as champions of Sunni orthodoxy against a century of Shia ascendancy and an Isma'ili underground. Through the Nizamiyya network they made Ash'ari theology the establishment position, endowed the four law schools, and backed a Sunni creed the caliph al-Qadir had issued in 1018. In Baghdad the Hanbali street, always the most combative, policed the result.
nodes.src: George Makdisi, 'The Sunni Revival' (1973); Daphna Ephrat, 'A Learned Society in a Period of Transition' (2000).

nodes.label: al-Ghazali at the Nizamiyya
nodes.full: Nizam al-Mulk appointed al-Ghazali, then in his early thirties, to the most prestigious chair in the Sunni world, the Baghdad Nizamiyya. Four years later, in a crisis of faith and nerve, he abandoned it to live as a wandering ascetic. He returned to write the Revival of the Religious Sciences, which folded law, Ash'ari theology and disciplined Sufism into a single mainstream — the shape Sunni Islam has kept.
nodes.src: al-Ghazali, 'al-Munqidh min al-Ḍalāl' and 'Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn'; Frank Griffel, 'Al-Ghazālī's Philosophical Theology' (2009).

nodes.label: Sufism becomes institutional
nodes.full: In these centuries Sufism stopped being a loose current of individual masters and became organised orders with lodges, lineages, rule-books and property. The tomb and lodge of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani in Baghdad became the centre of the Qadiriyya, the first of the great worldwide orders; the Suhrawardiyya grew from another Baghdad lodge, and its head served as al-Nasir's roving ambassador.
nodes.src: Abu Hafs Umar al-Suhrawardi, 'ʿAwārif al-Maʿārif'; J. Spencer Trimingham, 'The Sufi Orders in Islam' (1971).

nodes.label: The war on Isma'ilism
nodes.full: The Nizari 'new preaching', run from Alamut, was treated as an existential threat: al-Ghazali wrote a book-length refutation at the caliph's request, the madrasa curriculum was partly built to answer it, and Seljuk armies besieged its castles for decades. The intellectual and the military campaigns ran together for a century and a half, and both were finished only when the Mongols took Alamut in 1256.
nodes.src: al-Ghazali, 'Faḍāʾiḥ al-Bāṭiniyya'; Farhad Daftary, 'The Assassin Legends' (1994).

nodes.label: The Jews and Christians of Iraq, diminished
nodes.full: The Jewish academies of Iraq, the supreme authority of world Judaism for six centuries, faded after the last great gaon, Hai, died in 1038, and the centre of Jewish learning moved to Spain and the Rhineland. The community itself was still large — the traveller Benjamin of Tudela counted tens of thousands in Baghdad around 1170, and an exilarch still rode to court in state — but it was no longer the head of the body.
nodes.src: Benjamin of Tudela, 'Sefer ha-Massaʿot' (tr. Adler); Robert Brody, 'The Geonim of Babylonia' (1998).

nodes.label: The Arabic silver age and the Persianate turn
nodes.full: Even as the Seljuk chancery went over to Persian, Arabic prose reached a late peak in Iraq: al-Hariri of Basra's Maqamat — fifty picaresque episodes in dazzling rhymed prose, a rogue talking his way through the cities of the Muslim world — became, after the Quran, the most copied and imitated Arabic book there was, and set the standard of learned style for seven centuries.
nodes.src: al-Hariri, 'Maqāmāt'; the earlier 'Maqāmāt' of al-Hamadhani; A. F. L. Beeston on the genre.

nodes.label: The Baghdad school of painting
nodes.full: Baghdad's copyists learned to illustrate, and produced the first real school of Arab painting: al-Wasiti's 1237 Maqamat, alive with markets, camel trains, courtrooms and mosques; illustrated fable books, herbals and machine manuals; a bright, observant, humane style. It was barely two generations old when the sack of 1258 destroyed its workshops and its patrons together.
nodes.src: Richard Ettinghausen, 'Arab Painting' (1962); the Maqāmāt of al-Ḥarīrī, BnF MS arabe 5847 (al-Wasiti, 1237).

nodes.label: The historians of the catastrophe
nodes.full: A remarkable generation of Iraqi and Jaziran historians wrote as the disaster gathered: the Hanbali preacher Ibn al-Jawzi and his grandson chronicling Baghdad month by month; Ibn al-Athir composing a history of the world whose account of the Mongol invasion opens by calling it the worst calamity to befall mankind; Yaqut finishing his vast geographical dictionary in the last years of peace.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, 'al-Kāmil fī al-Ta'rīkh'; Yaqut, 'Muʿjam al-Buldān'; D. S. Richards's translations of Ibn al-Athir.

nodes.label: The stone that survived
nodes.full: Almost nothing of Abbasid Baghdad stands, but the last century left a little: the Mustansiriyya madrasa of 1234, the one major building of the caliphs still on its feet; the so-called tomb of Zubayda with its honeycombed brick cone; the Abbasid Palace; and, out at Kazimayn and Samarra and Najaf, the great Shia shrine complexes, rebuilt again and again in glazed brick and gold.
nodes.src: K. A. C. Creswell & James Allan, 'A Short Account of Early Muslim Architecture' (1989); Yasser Tabbaa, 'The Transformation of Islamic Art' (2001).

nodes.label: The Book of Songs and the theory of music
nodes.full: Buyid Baghdad produced the 'Book of Songs', al-Isfahani's twenty-volume anthology that preserves the words, tunes, singers and gossip of three centuries of Arabic song and is a main source for the whole culture. Three centuries later the city's librarian and court musician Safi al-Din al-Urmawi wrote the definitive account of the Arab modal system — and lived through the sack to teach it to the Mongols' governors.
nodes.src: Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani, 'Kitāb al-Aghānī'; Safi al-Din al-Urmawi, 'Kitāb al-Adwār'; Owen Wright, 'The Modal System of Arab and Persian Music' (1978).

nodes.label: The last Baghdad Aristotelians
nodes.full: The study of Greek logic and metaphysics had a last home in Baghdad in the Christian school of Yahya ibn Adi and his pupils and the salon of Abu Sulayman al-Sijistani. But the madrasa gave philosophy no chair, and the great work moved elsewhere — to the Iranian courts with Ibn Sina, and to Muslim Spain with Ibn Bajja and Ibn Rushd. Iraq, which had launched Arabic philosophy, largely stopped doing it.
nodes.src: al-Tawhidi, 'al-Imtāʿ wa-l-Muʾānasa'; Joel Kraemer, 'Humanism in the Renaissance of Islam' (1986).

nodes.label: The Buyid library culture and the Fihrist
nodes.full: Buyid Baghdad was a bibliophile's city. The vizier Sabur ibn Ardashir founded a public library and academy stocked with more than ten thousand manuscripts; other libraries stood in the palaces and the mosques; and the bookseller Ibn al-Nadim compiled the Fihrist, a catalogue of every work he could find or hear of that had been written in Arabic — a snapshot of the whole tradition just before the losses began.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Nadim, 'al-Fihrist' (tr. Dodge); Youssef Eche, 'Les bibliothèques arabes publiques et semi-publiques' (1967).

nodes.label: al-Ghazali against the philosophers
nodes.full: In the Incoherence of the Philosophers al-Ghazali argued that on three points — the eternity of the world, God's knowledge of particulars, and the resurrection of the body — the followers of Aristotle contradicted revelation so plainly that they had left Islam. It was the most weighty single blow struck in the long argument between reason and faith, and it was answered, a lifetime later, from Córdoba by Ibn Rushd.
nodes.src: al-Ghazali, 'Tahāfut al-Falāsifa' (tr. Marmura); Ibn Rushd's 'Tahāfut al-Tahāfut'.

nodes.label: The last great generation of Buyid science
nodes.full: Around the Buyid courts worked one more brilliant cohort of mathematicians and astronomers — al-Buzjani, who developed trigonometry and observed at a Baghdad observatory; al-Sijzi; al-Karaji, who freed algebra from geometry. After them the leading edge of the exact sciences shifted to Iran and Central Asia, and the observatory tradition was refounded not in Baghdad but at Maragha, in 1259, the year after the sack.
nodes.src: Roshdi Rashed, 'The Development of Arabic Mathematics' (1994); George Saliba, 'Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance' (2007).

nodes.label: The rational sciences narrowed
nodes.full: As the madrasa took over higher learning, theology became a fixed scholastic discipline — Ash'ari, taught from set texts — and the logic of the philosophers was folded into the curriculum while their metaphysics was walled off as unbelief. Free rational theology in the Mu'tazili mould survived mainly among the Twelver Shia and the Jewish academies. The space for open speculation in Sunni Iraq narrowed.
nodes.src: Robert Wisnovsky, 'The Nature and Scope of Arabic Philosophical Commentary in Post-Classical Islam' (2004); George Makdisi, 'The Rise of Colleges' (1981).

nodes.label: The end of the Sawad
nodes.full: The canal system that had made Iraq the richest land on earth began to fail. A wartime diversion of the Nahrawan around 937 was never properly repaired; more breaks followed; the wars and the tax-farmers gave no one the means or the motive to fix them. Archaeological survey of the Diyala plains shows settled sites falling by roughly two-thirds between the ninth century and the thirteenth. Iraq stopped feeding itself.
nodes.src: Robert McC. Adams, 'Land Behind Baghdad' (1965); Peter Verkinderen, 'Waterways of Iraq and Iran' (2015).

nodes.label: The trade axis shifts to the Red Sea
nodes.full: With Egypt strong and the Gulf disturbed, the great India trade re-routed away from the Basra–Baghdad corridor and through Aden, the Red Sea and Cairo. The letters of the Cairo Geniza track the shift merchant by merchant. Siraf declined, Basra shrank, and Baghdad found itself off the main artery of the world's commerce for the first time in four hundred years.
nodes.src: S. D. Goitein, 'A Mediterranean Society' vol. I (1967); Eliyahu Ashtor, 'A Social and Economic History of the Near East in the Middle Ages' (1976).

nodes.label: The militarised land
nodes.full: When the revenue of a district belonged to the soldier posted there, and passed to his son, the man on the ground had every reason to take the maximum this year and none to spend on next year's water. The peasantry was squeezed, the dikes went unmended, and villages emptied. The whole political economy of the Seljuk and post-Seljuk order worked against the recovery of Iraqi agriculture.
nodes.src: Marshall Hodgson, 'The Venture of Islam' vol. II (1974); Claude Cahen on the iqṭāʿ.

nodes.label: Baghdad contracts
nodes.full: Over three centuries the city shrank drastically. The Round City was gone; the west bank was mostly abandoned gardens and rubble; the built-up area and the population fell to perhaps a tenth of the ninth-century peak. By 1250 Baghdad was a large provincial town wearing the memory of a metropolis. The Mongols in 1258 destroyed a city that was already a shadow of itself.
nodes.src: Guy Le Strange, 'Baghdad During the Abbasid Caliphate' (1900); Jacob Lassner (1970).

nodes.label: The pilgrimage and shrine economy
nodes.full: What commerce Iraq kept ran on movement of people as much as goods: the hajj caravans that still mustered at Kufa and Baghdad while the desert road stayed safe, the steady flow of Shia pilgrims and their offerings to the shrines of Najaf, Karbala and Kazimayn, the date exports of Basra, and the caravans that linked Baghdad to Aleppo and to Tabriz. Reduced, but not dead.
nodes.src: Yaqut, 'Muʿjam al-Buldān'; the pilgrimage geography in Ibn Jubayr's 'Riḥla'.

nodes.label: The fragility of a hydraulic society
nodes.full: The Sawad's canals were not a fixed asset but a process — silt dredged every year, head-works rebuilt, the wandering rivers wrestled back into their beds — and the process needed a rich, unified central state to organise the labour and the money. Once the iqta broke that state, the network degraded past the point where anyone could repair it piecemeal. The physical system and the political system fell together.
nodes.src: Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); Michael Morony, 'Landholding and Social Change' (1994).

nodes.label: The four-iwan plan and the muqarnas vault
nodes.full: The Seljuks brought Iraq a new architecture: the courtyard building with a great vaulted hall on each of its four sides, used for the madrasa and the mosque, and the muqarnas — the honeycomb of small niches that carries the eye, and the load, from a square room up to a dome or down from a portal. The Mustansiriyya and the conical hood of the 'tomb of Zubayda' are the Baghdad examples.
nodes.src: Yasser Tabbaa, 'The Transformation of Islamic Art during the Sunni Revival' (2001).

nodes.label: The automata and instrument tradition
nodes.full: Just north of Iraq, at the Artuqid court of the Jazira, al-Jazari wrote in 1206 the fullest medieval book on machines: elaborate water-clocks and automata, water-raising devices, and a twin-cylinder pump driven by a true crankshaft — an early appearance of that mechanism anywhere. Baghdad's brass-inlay workshops and astrolabe makers belonged to the same technical world, which the sack scattered.
nodes.src: al-Jazari, 'Kitāb fī Maʿrifat al-Ḥiyal al-Handasiyya' (tr. Donald Hill, 1974).

nodes.label: The book industry and its destruction
nodes.full: Baghdad stayed a great centre of papermaking and of the copying trade, and the illustrated manuscript reached its height there in the last decades. All of it depended on the accumulated libraries — the raw material of every new copy. When the Mongols emptied the libraries into the Tigris in 1258, the loss was not just of books but of the capacity to make more of what had been in them.
nodes.src: Jonathan Bloom, 'Paper Before Print' (2001); the library destruction in Ibn Khaldun and later tradition.

nodes.label: The Turkmen migration
nodes.full: Behind the Seljuk sultans came the Oghuz Turkmen themselves, tribe after tribe, spreading over the pastures of Azerbaijan, the Jazira, the Syrian steppe and Anatolia. Northern Iraq's grazing land and its armies were permanently changed: a Turkish-speaking pastoral population settled in, and the Turkish mounted soldier — tribal levy or bought slave — became the basis of every state in the region for centuries.
nodes.src: Claude Cahen, 'Pre-Ottoman Turkey' (1968); A. C. S. Peacock, 'Early Seljūq History' (2010).

nodes.label: The Crusades, seen from Baghdad
nodes.full: When the Franks took Jerusalem in 1099, the delegations that came to Baghdad for help got sympathy and no army; the caliph had none to give and the sultan other priorities. The counter-crusade was built instead from Mosul and Aleppo — Zangi, then Nur al-Din, then Saladin, who took Egypt, ended the rival Fatimid caliphate, and ruled in the name of the Abbasid in Baghdad without ever taking orders from him.
nodes.src: Carole Hillenbrand, 'The Crusades: Islamic Perspectives' (1999); Ibn al-Athir, 'al-Kāmil'.

nodes.label: The Ilkhanate and the Mongol world
nodes.full: After 1258 Iraq was a province of the Ilkhanate, a Mongol state centred in Azerbaijan and joined to an empire that reached China and Russia. Its first rulers leaned toward their Christian and Buddhist subjects: in 1287 the Ilkhan sent Rabban Sauma, a Turkic Christian monk born near Beijing, as an envoy to the Pope and the kings of Europe. In 1295 the Ilkhan Ghazan converted to Islam, and the balance shifted again.
nodes.src: the 'History of Mar Yahballaha and Rabban Sauma' (tr. Montgomery); Judith Pfeiffer (ed.), 'Politics, Patronage and the Transmission of Knowledge in 13th–15th Century Tabriz' (2014).

nodes.label: The faith networks redirected
nodes.full: Iraqi Jewry stopped being the head of the body: the authority of the geonim passed to Qayrawan, al-Andalus and the Rhineland, and the flow of legal questions and answers reversed. The Church of the East, by contrast, reached its greatest extent — metropolitan sees at Samarkand, Kashgar and Khanbaliq, and whole Turkic and Mongol tribes, the Kerait and the Öngüd, adhering to it — even as its Iraqi base weakened.
nodes.src: Robert Brody, 'The Geonim of Babylonia' (1998); Ian Gillman & Hans-Joachim Klimkeit, 'Christians in Asia before 1500' (1999).

nodes.label: Baghdad as a memory and a magnet
nodes.full: Even shrunken, the city pulled people to it. Travellers came to look — Benjamin of Tudela, Ibn Jubayr — students came to the Mustansiriyya from across the Sunni world, and Sufi pilgrims came to the tomb of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani. The idea of Baghdad as the seat of the caliphate held the Muslim imagination long after the reality had thinned, which is why the news of 1258 landed as it did, everywhere at once.
nodes.src: Ibn Jubayr, 'Riḥla'; Nassima Neggaz on the memory of the fall of Baghdad.

nodes.label: Caliph and sultan, permanently apart
nodes.full: The settlement worked out in Buyid and Seljuk Baghdad became the standing form of Sunni political order: religious legitimacy belongs to the caliph, coercive power to the sultan, the two offices distinct and each incomplete without the other. It outlived the Abbasids by centuries — later sultans, Mamluk and Ottoman, still sought the caliphal seal — and was only formally dissolved in 1924.
nodes.src: Patricia Crone, 'God's Rule: Government and Islam' (2004); Ann Lambton, 'State and Government in Medieval Islam' (1981).

nodes.label: From the centre of the world to a march
nodes.full: These three centuries are the arc of Iraq's fall from primacy. It began them holding the capital of the largest empire on earth; it ended them a depopulated, canal-less frontier province ruled from Azerbaijan by Mongols. The tax base was gone, the great city was a tenth of its old size, the soldiery was foreign, and the trade of the world had moved to another river. The sack of 1258 was the last line, not the whole page.
nodes.src: Marshall Hodgson, 'The Venture of Islam' vol. II (1974); Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984), on the long trajectory.

nodes.label: The plural society thins and hardens
nodes.full: Two shifts ran through the period. The Jewish and Christian share of the population fell steadily — conversion, emigration, the occasional pogrom — so that a society that had been perhaps a third non-Muslim in 1000 was much less so by 1250. And among Muslims the Sunni–Shia line, drawn into the city's map and calendar under the Buyids, hardened into the sectarian geography Baghdad and the shrine cities still carry.
nodes.src: Richard Bulliet, 'Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period' (1979); Simha Sabari, 'Mouvements populaires à Bagdad' (1981).

nodes.label: The end of the Abbasid Caliphate
nodes.full: The killing of al-Musta'sim closed a line of thirty-seven caliphs and five hundred years, and with it the last institutional form of the idea that the Muslims were one community under one head. The Mamluks of Egypt soon installed a powerless Abbasid in Cairo to lend their sultans a blessing, but the thing itself was over. Iraq would not be the seat of a state again until the twentieth century.
nodes.src: John Andrew Boyle, 'The Death of the Last ʿAbbāsid Caliph' (1961); P. M. Holt, 'The Structure of Government in the Mamluk Sultanate' (1975), on the Cairo shadow caliphate.

nodes.label: Adud al-Dawla
nodes.full: The Buyid amir at the dynasty's summit: the first ruler since the early caliphs to be styled King of Kings, master of Iraq and much of Iran. He rebuilt Baghdad after flood and fire, endowed a great hospital run by two dozen physicians, repaired dams and dug canals, and kept a court of poets and astronomers — a Persian Shia governing a Sunni Arab city through a caliph who did as he was told.
nodes.src: Miskawayh, 'Tajārib al-Umam'; Harold Bowen & C. E. Bosworth, 'ʿAḍud al-Dawla' in EI2.

nodes.label: Nizam al-Mulk
nodes.full: For thirty years the Persian vizier ran the Seljuk empire for two sultans who mostly let him. He built the state madrasa system, regularised the land-assignment army, wrote the age's classic manual of statecraft, and kept a network of informants on everyone including the sultan. In 1092, on the road near Nihavand, a young man in the dress of a petitioner stabbed him — the Nizaris' first and most famous killing.
nodes.src: Nizam al-Mulk, 'Siyāsatnāma'; the assassination in Ibn al-Athir and Rashid al-Din.

nodes.label: al-Ghazali
nodes.full: He held the most prestigious chair in Sunni Islam at thirty-three, and at thirty-seven he could not go on: he left Baghdad, his family and his post, and spent years as a poor wanderer between Damascus, Jerusalem and Mecca. When he returned to teaching he wrote the Revival of the Religious Sciences, which made a disciplined mysticism part of mainstream Sunni practice and remains, after the Quran and hadith, among the most read books in Islam.
nodes.src: al-Ghazali, 'al-Munqidh min al-Ḍalāl'; Kenneth Garden, 'The First Islamic Reviver' (2014).

nodes.label: The exilarch of Benjamin of Tudela's Baghdad
nodes.full: A Spanish Jewish traveller who reached Baghdad around 1170 left a portrait of the head of the exile, the Rosh ha-Golah: escorted to the caliph's court by riders calling 'make way for our lord the son of David,' confirmed in authority over the Jews of Persia, Central Asia and Yemen, rich, learned, and treated with honour. It was the last grandeur of an office that ran back to the Babylonian captivity.
nodes.src: Benjamin of Tudela, 'Sefer ha-Massaʿot' (tr. Marcus Nathan Adler, 1907).

nodes.label: al-Musta'sim, the last caliph
nodes.full: The thirty-seventh Abbasid: devout, a fine calligrapher, fond of music, and served by a court that spent its energy on its own feuds. Warned for years that the Mongols were coming, he could not decide whether to fight or submit, and did neither in time. Taken alive, made to watch the sack, and then — so that no royal blood should touch the earth — wrapped in a carpet and trampled to death by horsemen.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din, 'Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh'; Bar Hebraeus, 'Chronography'.
